text.p: The explosive component and propellant of an M55 nerve gas rocket have been destroyed at a U.S. Army-certified commercial laboratory through a chemical process known as solvated electron technology -- or SET process -- developed by Teledyne-Commodore LLC, it said.
Teledyne-Commodore is a joint venture of Allegheny Teledyne Inc and Commodore Applied Technologies Inc.
The successful completion of the test was critical to competing for the Alternative Technology Program under consideration by the Army for the destruction of stored munitions, the company explained.
It said the SET process is "significantly more cost-effective than other technologies."

"The demilitarization of these materials using methods other than incineration has been one of the most difficult tasks in the Department of Defense Chemical Weapons Program," said Teledyne-Commodore president Gerald G. Watson.
"We consider this a major breakthrough in the search for alternative non-thermal technologies capable of destroying explosive materials in chemical weapons," Watson said.
A retired Major General, Watson was the Army's chief chemical officer.
The SET process renders explosives inert and destroys any chemical agent that may have contaminated the explosives and propellant, the venture said.

Department of Defense chemical demilitarization measurements of success include neutralization of a wide spectrum of military chemical agents, decontamination of metal components, elimination of agent-contaminated dunnage material and destruction of the explosives in chemical munitions.

"With the successful results of this explosives test, SET has now met all four of these requirements," Watson said. "This is critical to competing for the Alternative Technology Program under consideration by the Army for the destruction of assembled munitions."

Chemical agents have been stored for over 40 years on eight U.S. Army bases in the continental U.S. Currently, munitions are also stored on Johnston Island in the Pacific. These munitions were removed from forward deployed depots in Europe and the Far East. ((-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610.))
